title: a path
hookLine: a path — eight parts, a life
tomorrow: five, and they read like kindness

cards: A mechanic tells you the car has a problem, and walks off. A friend says you seem stressed, and changes the subject. Being told what's wrong and then left there is almost worse than not knowing.
The first three truths could have been like that. There is dukkha. It comes from thirst.
The Buddha didn't leave it there. The fourth truth isn't an idea at all. It's directions.

teach.b: The fourth noble truth is magga, the path. The way that leads to the end of dukkha.
It has eight parts, so it's called the noble eightfold path. Here they are, quickly. Right view.
Right intention. Right speech. Right action.
Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness, the sati from day three.
Right concentration. The word translated right is samma, and it's gentler than it sounds in English. It means whole, complete, well-tuned, the way a chord is right.
Not right as opposed to wrong answers on a test. Right the way a thing fits. In one of the old discourses, a nun named Dhammadinna sorts the eight into three bundles.
Wisdom: seeing clearly and meaning well. Conduct: how you speak, act and earn a living. And meditation: effort, mindfulness, concentration.
Notice what that means. Most of the path isn't sitting on a cushion. It's how you talk to your sister and how you make your money.
And here's what people often get wrong. The eight aren't steps you finish one at a time, like levels.

teach.h: SPOKES OF A WHEEL, NOT STEPS.
teach.b: They're more like the eight spokes of a wheel, and many Buddhists read the eight-spoked wheel that way. They turn together. A little honesty helps meditation.

teach.h: THE BEST OF WAYS IS THE EIGHTFOLD.
teach.b: One old verse says it plainly: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words." The four words are the four truths you now know. The eightfold way is how you walk them.

how: Buddhists practice the eightfold path as a whole way of life: keeping ethical precepts in speech, action and work, meditating, and studying the teaching; the eight-spoked wheel, the dharmachakra, is one of Buddhism's most common symbols.

games.q: what's inside the path — tap the pairs.

s: you finish the eight steps one at a time
they turn together, like spokes of a wheel.
most of the path is about more than meditation
only three of the eight are meditation; speech, action and livelihood sit right in the middle.
samma means right as in 'correct answer'
it's closer to whole, complete, well-tuned, the way a thing fits.

games.q: you want to start the eightfold path today. where do you begin?
o: right view. you can't do the rest until it's perfect.
right concentration. meditation first, life later.
games.why: the eight parts support each other like spokes. many teachers say you can start anywhere: a little honesty helps meditation, and a little meditation helps honesty.

practice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. Pick just one spoke of the wheel.
Maybe speech: one thing you'd like to say more kindly. Maybe action: one small harm you'd like to skip. Maybe livelihood: one moment at work you'd like to do honestly.
Hold that one spoke in mind, and breathe with it. Nobody walks all eight at once. One step is still walking.

wordCard.voice: The eightfold path. The fourth noble truth: eight parts, wisdom, conduct and meditation, turning together like a wheel. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Pali: the noble eightfold path. magga, path; aṭṭhaṅgika, eight-limbed.

carryVoice: Your line: walk. The truths are something you walk, not something you believe. Day eleven.
